unit.title: Weld using gas metal arc welding process (GMAW) – metal inert gas (MIG)

summary: This unit teaches you to weld mild steel with gas metal arc welding (GMAW), usually called MIG welding, where a wire fed from a spool melts in an arc under a shield of gas. You will learn to work safely with the arc, fume and gas cylinders; set up the machine, the gas and the wire; choose and adjust the voltage and wire feed speed; make butt and fillet welds with good gun technique; and inspect your welds, put faults right, look after the equipment and report problems.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches **gas metal arc welding (GMAW)**, known in the workshop as **MIG welding**: setting up the machine, the shielding gas and the wire, choosing the settings, making butt and fillet welds on mild steel, and checking, cleaning up and reporting.

MIG welding is fast, clean and easy to learn, so it is the main process in many Jamaican fabrication shops and factories: trailer frames, security grilles, hurricane shutters, steel furniture, vehicle bodies and repairs, racking, tanks and light structural work. It welds thin sheet without burning through, needs no chipping between runs, and lets you weld a long joint without stopping to change electrodes.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. You will weld mild steel sheet and plate, mostly with 0.8 mm or 0.9 mm ER70S-6 wire and an argon and carbon dioxide gas mix.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely
Control the hazards of arc light, electric shock, fume, shielding gas, fire and hot metal; wear the right PPE; protect the people around you.
Set up the gas
Choose the right gas, secure the cylinder, fit the regulator/flowmeter, leak-test it and set the flow.
Set up the wire feed and gun
Fit the right drive rolls, load and thread the wire, set the roll pressure and spool brake, and fit the right contact tip and nozzle.
Choose and adjust the settings
Set the polarity, voltage and wire feed speed from the chart, test on scrap, and adjust from what the arc and bead show you.
Prepare and weld the joint
Clean, fit up and tack the parts; hold the right stick-out and gun angles; make butt and fillet welds in the flat and horizontal positions.
Inspect and correct
Check welds by eye and with a fillet gauge, name the faults and their causes, and say what you will change.
Care for the equipment and report
Clean the gun, check the cables and parts, shut down safely, and report faults, damage and incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the process, safety, fume, gases and cylinders, equipment, wire feed, settings, technique, defects and maintenance.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words such as liner, post-flow, bird's nest and MAG) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: fillet welds on tee joints in the horizontal position (2F) in 6 mm plate, and a full station set-up (regulator and wire) followed by a butt weld and a lap weld in 3 mm sheet. The assessor watches your set-up, PPE, test welds and clean-up, not only the finished welds.

blocks.note: Many marks come from set-up and explaining what you do. Practise saying each step as you do it: why the rolls must match the wire, why the cable lies straight, why you test on scrap.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: In MIG welding, an electric arc burns between a **solid wire** and the work. The wire is fed continuously from a spool, through the gun cable and out of the **contact tip**, at a speed you set. The arc melts the end of the wire and the edges of the joint into a **weld pool**. A **shielding gas**, fed through the same gun, flows out of the nozzle round the arc and keeps the air away from the hot metal. There is no flux and no slag to chip.

flow: Mains supply (220 V for most workshop machines; some small machines run on 110 V)
Power source: gives a steady welding voltage, DC
Wire feeder: drive rolls push the wire from the spool into the gun cable
Gun cable: carries the wire (inside the liner), the gas, the welding current and the trigger wires
Gun: the contact tip passes the current into the wire; the nozzle directs the gas
Arc and weld pool, shielded by the gas
Work lead and clamp: carry the current back to the machine

head: Name
What it means
rows: GMAW
Gas metal arc welding: the official name of the process
MIG
Metal inert gas: welding with an **inert** gas such as argon, which does not react with the weld; used for aluminium and other non-ferrous metals
MAG
Metal active gas: welding with an **active** gas such as carbon dioxide (CO2), or argon mixed with CO2, which takes part in the arc; used for steel. In the workshop most people still call it MIG.
Semi-automatic
The machine feeds the wire at a set speed; you guide the gun along the joint by hand

head: Strengths
Limits
rows: Fast: long welds without stopping
No slag to chip, little clean-up
Thin sheet and thicker plate with the same machine
Easy to learn for flat and horizontal work
Wind blows the gas shield away, so outdoor work needs screens
The joint must be clean: there is no flux to deal with rust and dirt
The gun and cable are bulky in tight places
On thick plate, low settings can leave welds that look good but are not fused (cold lap)

blocks.note: A light breeze is enough to blow the gas shield away. If you cannot screen the work from the wind on site, use a process that does not rely on a gas shield, as your supervisor decides.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: MIG welding has the same main hazards as other arc welding: **arc radiation**, **electric shock**, **fume**, **fire** and **burns**. It adds two of its own: **shielding gas** that can push the air out of a closed space, and a **wire** that shoots out of the gun when you press the trigger.

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Arc radiation

The MIG arc is very bright and rich in ultraviolet (UV), especially with argon mixes. With no smoke to dim it, it burns bare skin like severe sunburn within minutes and causes arc eye. Light reflects off shiny metal and pale walls.
Helmet with the right shade
All skin covered, collar buttoned
Screens round the bay
Warn others before you strike
Electric shock
The wire, contact tip, drive rolls and spool are live whenever the trigger is pressed. Sweat and rain let current through your skin.
Dry gloves and clothing
Cables and gun checked before use
Feeder cover closed while welding
Switch off and isolate before opening the feeder or changing parts
Fume and gases
MIG gives off a lot of fume: tiny particles of metal and metal oxide. The arc also makes ozone, and CO2 shielding gas can break down into carbon monoxide.
Local extraction close to the arc
Head out of the plume
Coatings removed
Respirator where needed
Shielding gas
Argon and CO2 have no smell. A leak in a small or low space pushes out the oxygen, and a person can pass out without warning.
Cylinder valve closed when not in use
Good ventilation
No welding in tanks or pits without proper controls
Wire
When you press the trigger, the wire comes out of the gun fast and its end is sharp. It can pierce skin or an eye.
Never point the gun at yourself or anyone else
Keep fingers away from the tip and the drive rolls
Fire and burns
Spatter and sparks fly several metres and lodge in rags, wood and gaps. Welded metal stays hot long after it stops glowing.
Burnables cleared or covered
Extinguisher at hand
Pliers or tongs; hot work marked HOT
Fire watch after the job

blocks.note: Shade charts give about 10 to 11 for most short-circuit MIG work on steel, and 12 to 13 for the higher currents of spray transfer. Follow the chart for your helmet and your instructor. If your eyes ache or you see spots after welding, the shade is too light.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use **local exhaust ventilation (LEV)**: an extractor hood or arm placed **close to the arc** so it draws the fume away from your face before you breathe it.

Do not let the extractor or a fan blow strongly across the weld. A strong draught blows away the shielding gas and causes porosity. Place the hood to the side of or just above the arc, not blowing at it.
Keep your head out of the plume that rises from the arc.
Remove paint, oil, plastic coatings and zinc from the weld area first. **Galvanised** steel gives off zinc fume that causes metal fume fever, a flu-like illness a few hours later.
Stainless steel fume contains chromium and nickel, which are especially harmful: use extraction every time.
Never use chlorinated degreasing solvents near the arc: its UV can turn their vapour into a poisonous gas.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat, shops open their doors and run big standing fans. A fan blowing across the bench keeps you cool but strips the gas shield off the weld. Point fans at the welder from behind or to the side, away from the arc, and put up a screen between the open door and the bench.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Area: screens up, anything that burns cleared, extinguisher ready, extraction on, floor dry
You: full PPE, dry gloves, lighters out of your pockets
Equipment: mains cable, gun cable, work lead and clamp undamaged; cylinder chained; gas flowing at the set rate
Job: clean, fitted and tacked; work clamp on clean metal close to the joint
Test: run a bead on scrap of the same thickness and adjust
Warn the people nearby, lower your helmet, and weld

sections.title: The MIG set: power source, wire feeder and gun

blocks.p: A MIG power source is a **constant voltage (CV)** machine. You set the voltage, and the machine holds it steady while the current rises and falls as needed. This makes the arc **self-adjusting**: if your hand moves closer and the arc gets shorter, the current rises at once and the wire burns off faster, bringing the arc back to length. That is why you can weld smoothly with a wire that is fed at a fixed speed.

Solid steel wire is welded on **direct current, electrode positive (DCEP)**: the gun is connected to the positive (+) terminal and the work lead to the negative (−). This gives a stable arc, good penetration and little spatter. (Some gasless flux-cored wires run on DC electrode negative; that belongs to another unit. Always check the polarity the wire box gives.)

Many modern **inverter** machines are **synergic**: you choose the wire, the gas and the thickness, and one knob sets the voltage and wire speed together. You can still trim them. Older machines have a voltage switch or knob and a separate wire speed knob. Read the rating plate for the supply (most need 220 V) and the **duty cycle**, the minutes in every 10 the machine can weld at a given current.

head: Part
Its job
rows: Spool hub and brake
Holds the spool; the brake stops the spool spinning on (overrunning) when the wire stops, so loose coils do not spring off
Inlet guide
Leads the wire straight into the drive rolls
Drive rolls
Grip the wire and push it through the cable to the gun; the groove type and size must match the wire
Pressure arm and tension knob
Press the top roll onto the wire; set just tight enough to feed without slipping
Outlet guide
Leads the wire from the rolls into the gun cable's liner
Wire inch button and gas test button (on many machines)
Feed wire without welding or gas; run gas without feeding wire, to set the flow

head: Roll groove
Used for
Why
rows: V-groove
Solid steel and stainless steel wire
Hard wire: the V grips it firmly on two sides
U-groove
Aluminium and other soft wire
A V would bite into and shave soft wire; a U supports it
Knurled (toothed) groove
Flux-cored wire
The teeth grip the wire without crushing the tube

blocks.note: Every roll groove is made for one wire size, stamped on the roll (for example 0.8 or 0.9). Many rolls have two grooves: turn the roll to put the right one in line with the wire.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Part
Its job
Check
rows: Liner
A flexible tube inside the gun cable that guides the wire from the feeder to the contact tip. Steel wire uses a steel coil liner; aluminium uses a plastic (PTFE or nylon) liner.
Right size for the wire; not kinked or clogged with dust and copper flakes
Contact tip
Passes the welding current into the wire as it slides through
Same size as the wire (0.9 mm wire, 0.9 mm tip)
Hole not worn oval and not blocked with spatter
Screwed in tight
Gas diffuser (tip holder)
Holds the tip and spreads the gas evenly into the nozzle
Gas holes clear
Nozzle (shroud)
Directs the gas round the arc and the pool
Free of spatter; not dented; fitted tight
Trigger
Starts the gas, the wire and the current together
Works cleanly; switch not sticking
Gun cable
Carries the wire, gas, current and trigger wires
No cuts, burns or crushed sections; laid out without tight bends

blocks.p: The **work lead** (often called the earth lead) carries the current from the work back to the machine and completes the circuit. Fix the clamp to clean, bare metal on the job, as close to the weld as you can. A clamp on rust or paint, or a loose connection, gives an unsteady arc and gets hot. It is not a safety earth: the machine's safety earth is in its mains cable.

The main job of the shielding gas is to **keep the air away from the arc and the molten weld pool**. Air contains oxygen and nitrogen, which would make the weld porous and brittle. The gas also affects how the arc behaves, how the metal crosses the arc, the shape of the bead and the amount of spatter.

head: Gas
Used for
Points to know
rows: Carbon dioxide (CO2), 100%
Mild steel
An active gas: deep penetration
More spatter and a rougher bead
Cheapest
Cannot give spray transfer
Argon with about 15–25% CO2 (for example "Ar 75% / CO2 25%")
Mild steel, the usual choice for short-circuit work
Smoother arc and bead, less spatter than CO2
The gas used in this unit's practicals
Argon with a little CO2 or oxygen (about 2–10%)
Spray transfer on thicker steel; stainless steel with the low-CO2 mixes
Argon-rich mixes are needed for spray transfer
Argon, 100%
Aluminium, copper and other non-ferrous metals (true MIG)
Gives a poor, unsteady bead on steel: not used for steel

ul: Indoors, in still air, a flow of about **10–20 litres per minute** is usual for steel. Use the figure on the welding procedure or job sheet.
Set it with gas flowing: press the gas test button, or press the trigger with the wire feed off as the machine allows, and read the flowmeter as its maker says.
**Too little** gas leaves the pool unprotected: porosity.
**Too much** gas is wasteful, and the fast, swirling stream can drag air into the shield, causing porosity too. Turning the gas up is not the cure for a draught: screening the work is.
**Pre-flow** starts the gas a moment before the arc, to clear the air from the gun and nozzle.
**Post-flow** keeps the gas flowing for a short time after the arc stops, to protect the cooling crater. Hold the gun over the end of the weld until it stops.
Keep cylinders **upright and chained** or strapped to a trolley or a wall, so they cannot fall. A falling cylinder can break its valve and fly like a rocket.
Move them on a trolley with the valve cap on. Never lift a cylinder by its valve, and never roll it along the floor on its side.
Keep them away from heat, sparks and the welding circuit: never strike an arc on a cylinder, and never let the gun or work lead touch it.
Read the **label** to know what gas is inside. Colours differ between suppliers and countries. If a cylinder has no readable label, do not use it: return it to the supplier.
Keep **CO2** cylinders upright: CO2 is stored as a liquid, and liquid reaching the regulator can freeze it.
Store spare cylinders in a ventilated, shaded, secure place, never in a closed back room or a pit.

flow: Check the cylinder label for the right gas, and chain the cylinder upright
Take off the cap; check that the valve outlet and the regulator thread are clean and undamaged, with no oil or grease
If the Centre's rules allow, stand to one side and open the valve for a moment to blow out dust, then close it
Fit the regulator/flowmeter made for that gas and tighten the nut with the correct spanner, without forcing it
Check that the flow adjuster is closed, stand to one side of the regulator, and open the cylinder valve slowly
Brush leak-detection fluid or soapy water on the joints and look for bubbles; never test with a flame
Connect the gas hose to the machine and set the flow

blocks.p: When CO2 leaves the cylinder it expands and cools sharply. On long welds or at high flow the regulator can **frost over and freeze**, and the gas flow drops or stops, causing porosity. The cure is a **heated CO2 regulator** (or a heater fitted ahead of it, as the maker supplies). Never pour water on a frozen regulator or hit it to free it.

blocks.note: Argon and CO2 are heavier than air and have no smell. A leak in a small room, a pit or a tank can push out the oxygen, and a person can collapse without warning. Close the cylinder valve when you stop welding, keep the area ventilated, and never weld inside a closed space without the controls your supervisor sets.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Welding wire: choosing, loading and feeding

blocks.p: The most common MIG wire for mild steel is **ER70S-6**. Its code tells you:

head: Part
Meaning
rows: ER
Electrode or Rod: it can be used as a MIG electrode wire or as a TIG filler rod
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
S
Solid wire (not flux-cored)
The chemistry. The -6 wire has extra manganese and silicon, which clean the weld pool, so it copes better with light mill scale and rust than the -3 wire, which suits clean steel

blocks.p: Common sizes are 0.6, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0 and 1.2 mm. Thin sheet uses 0.6–0.8 mm; general workshop work 0.8–0.9 mm; thicker plate 1.0–1.2 mm. Most steel wire is copper-coated to protect it from rust and help it feed.

ul: Keep spare spools in their sealed packing, in a clean, dry place off the floor.
Damp and salty air rust wire within days. Rusty wire feeds roughly, wears the tip and liner and causes porosity.
If the machine will not be used for a while, cover the spool or put it back in its bag.
Keep the label with the spool, so you always know what wire is on the machine.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, and salt air in coastal towns, rust bare steel wire quickly. Do not leave an opened spool on an idle machine with the feeder cover open for days.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Switch the machine off and isolate it before opening the wire feeder
Check the drive rolls: a V-groove of the same size as the wire; change or turn them if not
Fit the spool on its hub so it unwinds from the bottom towards the rolls (or as the machine shows), and fit the retaining clip or nut
Hold the wire end firmly so the spool cannot spring loose, cut off the bent end cleanly, and file off any sharp burr
Push the wire through the inlet guide, over the drive roll and into the outlet guide
Close the pressure arm and set the roll pressure
Lay the gun cable out straight; take off the nozzle and contact tip
Switch on, point the gun away from everyone, and press the inch button or trigger until the wire comes out of the gun
Fit a contact tip the same size as the wire, refit the nozzle and trim the wire to the right stick-out
Set the spool brake so the spool stops without spinning on

blocks.h: Roll pressure and the spool brake

head: Setting
Too low
Too high
rows: Drive roll pressure
The rolls slip; the wire feeds jerkily or stops; the arc is unsteady and the wire may burn back to the tip
The wire is squashed out of round, drags in the liner and tip, and can kink and tangle at the rolls (a bird's nest)
Spool brake
The spool runs on when the wire stops, and loose coils spring off and tangle
The rolls struggle to pull the wire off the spool; feeding is jerky

blocks.p: A good roll pressure feeds the wire smoothly, but if the wire is stopped at the gun, the rolls slip rather than crushing it into a tangle.

head: Fault
What you see
Common causes
What to do
rows: Bird's nest
A tangle of wire round the drive rolls
Wire stuck in the tip (burnback)
Kinked or clogged liner
Gun cable coiled tightly
Roll pressure too high
Tip too small
Isolate the machine, cut out the tangle, find and fix the cause, rethread
Burnback
The wire melts back and fuses to the contact tip
Stick-out held too short
Wire feed too slow for the voltage
Wire slipping or snagging in the feed
Wrong size or worn tip
Switch off, change or free the tip, and correct the cause
Erratic feed
The arc surges, pops and stops
Roll pressure wrong
Worn or dirty liner
Worn tip
Spool brake too tight
Rusty wire
Check the feed path from spool to tip, one part at a time

blocks.note: Keep the gun cable as straight as you can while welding. A cable coiled in tight loops, or bent sharply over the bench edge, makes the wire drag in the liner and is a common cause of poor feeding and bird's nests.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Aluminium wire is soft and bends easily, so it needs **U-groove** rolls, a **plastic (PTFE or nylon) liner**, light roll pressure and a short, straight gun cable. Many shops use a spool gun, with a small spool on the gun itself. Aluminium is welded with **pure argon**, and its surface oxide must be removed with a stainless steel brush kept only for aluminium, just before welding.

head: Setting
What it controls
Turn it up
Turn it down
rows: Wire feed speed (WFS)
The **current** (amps). More wire fed into the arc means more current is needed to melt it.
More amps, more heat, more weld metal, deeper penetration
Fewer amps; a smaller weld; too low gives poor fusion
Voltage
The **arc length**, and so the width and shape of the bead
Longer arc; wider, flatter bead; too high gives spatter, undercut and burnback
Shorter arc; narrower, taller bead; too low makes the wire stub into the plate

blocks.p: The two must be **in balance**: each wire speed has a voltage that suits it. A good short-circuit arc makes a steady, even crackle, like bacon frying in a pan.

blocks.h: Signs that the settings are wrong

head: What you see and hear
Likely cause
What to do
rows: The wire stubs into the plate and pushes the gun back
A tall, narrow, ropey bead sitting on top
Spatter
Voltage too low for the wire speed
Raise the voltage a little
A long, hissing arc; large drops; spatter
A wide, flat bead with undercut
The wire burns back towards the tip
Voltage too high for the wire speed
Lower the voltage a little
Too little weld metal; poor fusion
Thin plate looks fine but thick plate is not fused
Wire speed (current) too low for the thickness
Raise the wire speed, then rebalance the voltage
Burn-through on thin sheet; a large, runny pool
Wire speed and voltage too high for the thickness
Lower both, and travel a little faster
A steady crackle; an even bead with fine ripples, blending smoothly into the plate

Keep them; write them down

blocks.h: Finding the settings for a new job

flow: Check the drawing or welding procedure for the wire, the gas, the thickness and the joint
Read the starting settings from the chart inside the machine (often on the feeder door) or from the procedure
Weld a test bead on scrap of the same thickness, in the same position
Look at the bead and listen to the arc
Change one setting at a time, in small steps, and test again
Write down the settings that work, for next time

head: Steel thickness
Typical starting point (0.8–0.9 mm wire, argon/CO2 mix, short-circuit)
rows: About 15–17 V, about 50–90 A
3 mm
About 17–19 V, about 100–140 A
6 mm (fillet)
About 19–22 V, about 150–200 A

blocks.note: These are rough guide figures only. Machines, wires and gases differ: start from your machine's chart or the procedure, test on scrap, and follow the manufacturer's instructions and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The way the melted metal crosses from the wire to the pool is called the **transfer mode**. It depends mainly on the current, the voltage and the gas.

head: Mode
How it works
Settings and gas
Used for
Watch out for
rows: Short-circuit (dip)
The wire touches the pool about 20 to 200 times a second; each touch is a short circuit that melts off a small drop
Low voltage and current; CO2 or argon/CO2 mixes
Thin sheet, root runs, gaps, and **all positions**: the small pool freezes quickly
On thick plate it can leave **cold lap** (lack of fusion) that looks sound
Globular
Large drops, bigger than the wire, form and fall across the arc
Between short-circuit and spray; common with CO2 at higher currents
Flat and horizontal work where spatter does not matter
Heavy spatter and a rough bead; usually avoided
Spray
A fine stream of tiny drops crosses the arc without touching the pool
High voltage and current, above a transition current (often around 200 A); an argon-rich gas (about 80% argon or more)
Thicker plate: deep penetration, smooth bead, little spatter, fast
Only in the **flat** position and for **horizontal fillets**: the large, fluid pool would run out of other positions; very bright and hot, so PPE must be good

blocks.p: Some modern machines also offer **pulsed** transfer, which switches rapidly between a high and a low current. It gives spray-like drops with less heat, so it can be used out of position. Your instructor will tell you if your machine has it.

ul: Read the drawing or welding procedure: the material, the thickness, the joint, the weld size and the position.

Clean the joint and about 25 mm each side to **bright metal**: grind or brush off rust, mill scale and paint, and wipe off oil and grease. MIG has no flux, so dirt goes straight into the weld as **porosity** and **poor fusion**.
Fit the parts as the drawing says. Square-edge butt joints in thin sheet need a small, even gap (often about 1 mm for 3 mm sheet) or none, as the procedure gives. Tee and lap joints fit with no gap.
**Tack** each end, and at even spacing along long joints. Small tacks that fuse well are easy to weld over.
Fix the work clamp to clean metal close to the joint.

head: Code
Also called
What it is
rows: 1G
PA
Butt (groove) weld in the flat position: the plates lie flat and you weld from above
2G
PC
Butt weld in the horizontal position: the plates stand upright and the joint runs across
1F
PA
Fillet weld in the flat position: the joint is tilted so the weld lies in a trough with its face level
2F
PB
Fillet weld in the horizontal position: for example a tee joint with the base plate lying flat on the bench

blocks.note: A tee or lap joint lying flat on the bench is strictly a **horizontal** fillet (2F), because the weld sits in a corner against an upright face. Workshops often call a lap laid on the bench "flat". Follow the job sheet and your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Stick-out** (also called electrode extension) is the length of wire between the end of the contact tip and the arc. For short-circuit welding it is usually about **6–12 mm**, about 10 mm being a good habit; spray transfer uses a little more. Keep it steady.

head: Stick-out
What happens
rows: Too long
The wire is heated by its own resistance before it reaches the arc, so the current drops: less penetration, an unsteady arc, more spatter, and the nozzle is too far away to protect the pool with gas
Too short
The tip is close to the pool: spatter builds up in the nozzle and on the tip, the wire can burn back and fuse to the tip, and you cannot see the joint

blocks.p: The **travel angle** is the lean of the gun along the line of the weld: usually about **5–15°** from upright. The **work angle** is the angle of the gun across the joint.

head: Joint
Work angle
Points to watch
rows: Butt joint, flat (1G)
90°, square to the plates
Keep the wire on the centre of the joint; watch the back for penetration
Lap joint lying flat
About 60–70° from the bottom sheet, so the arc favours the bottom sheet
The thin top edge melts away easily: keep the wire on the root and the bottom sheet
Tee joint, horizontal (2F)
About 45° between the two plates, with the wire aimed into the root or very slightly onto the bottom plate
Undercut on the upright plate and overlap on the bottom plate
Thin part to thick part
Angle the arc more onto the thicker part
The thin part burns away if it takes the full arc

head: Technique
How
Result
rows: Push (forehand)
The gun leans back and the wire points ahead, the way you are travelling
A flatter, wider bead with a little less penetration; a good view of the joint and good gas cover. Usual for MIG on steel sheet and for aluminium.
Pull (drag, backhand)
The gun leans forward and the wire points back at the weld
A narrower, taller bead with a little more penetration

ul: Hold the gun at the right stick-out and angles with the wire just off the joint, lower your helmet, then press the trigger.
The start of a MIG weld is the coldest part. Start a little ahead on the joint line and come straight back over the start point, or pause briefly, so the start is fused.
Travel at a steady speed, keeping the arc on the **leading edge** of the pool. If the pool runs ahead of the arc, the arc lands on liquid metal instead of the plate and leaves lack of fusion.
At the end, pause briefly to fill the crater, release the trigger, and hold the gun over the weld until the post-flow stops.

head: Weld
Key points
rows: Butt weld in 3 mm sheet, flat
Small, even gap; tacked at each end
Work angle 90°, travel angle 5–15°, steady stick-out
Watch the pool sink through: penetration should show evenly on the back with no burn-through
Lap fillet in 3 mm sheet
Sheets clamped tight with no gap
Wire on the root, favouring the bottom sheet
Top edge fused but not melted away; no undercut on the top edge
Tee fillet in 6 mm plate, horizontal (2F)
Upright plate tacked square at each end
Work angle about 45°, travel angle 5–15°, usually pushing
Steady speed so the legs stay equal; fused into both plates and the root; crater filled

blocks.p: MIG puts heat in quickly, and thin sheet buckles easily. Tack often, clamp the work, keep runs short and spread them out (welding a short length here, then a short length at the other end), and balance the welds on opposite sides. Do not cool welds with water.

blocks.note: Cold lap is dangerous because a MIG weld can look neat while it is not fused to the plate. If you are welding thicker plate at low settings, ask your instructor to cut or break a test weld so you can see the fusion.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Let the weld cool, brush off loose spatter, and look at it in good light, from both ends and from the side.
Check fillet size with a **fillet gauge**: both legs equal and at least the size on the drawing.
Look for an even width and height, fine even ripples, and smooth blending into both plates at the toes.
Look for porosity, undercut, overlap, cracks (especially in the crater), burn-through and heavy spatter.
Check the **start and the end** carefully: faults are most common there.
Check the job is still square and to size, because the heat pulls parts out of line.
Mark faults with chalk, write your findings on the inspection sheet with the job number and your name, and report anything outside the drawing to your instructor.

blocks.h: Looking after the gun and machine

head: When
What to do
rows: Before use
Mains cable and plug undamaged; test tag in date if the Centre uses them
Gun cable, work lead and clamp: no cuts, burns or loose connections
Gas hose and fittings sound; cylinder chained
Contact tip the right size, not worn oval; nozzle and diffuser clean
Drive rolls the right type and size; wire feeding smoothly
While welding
Clean spatter from the nozzle regularly
Change a tip that is worn, blocked or has burnback
Keep the gun cable straight and off hot metal
Spatter in the nozzle

With the trigger released (or the machine off), remove it with **MIG pliers** (nozzle pliers) or a nozzle reamer; a light coat of anti-spatter gel or spray helps it fall off. Never tap the nozzle on the bench: you damage the gun.
When changing wire
With the machine isolated, blow dust and copper flakes out of the liner with dry compressed air as your instructor shows; replace a kinked or worn liner

flow: Finish the weld and fill the crater
Close the cylinder valve
Bleed the gas from the hose and regulator with the gas test button or the trigger, until the flowmeter reads zero
Switch off the machine, and at the mains if the Centre's rules say so
Clean spatter from the nozzle and tip; cut the wire back to a short stick-out
Cover or bag the spool if the machine will stand idle
Coil the gun cable and work lead in large, loose loops and hang them off the floor
Cool and mark hot work, sweep up, check for smouldering, and report any faults

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Damaged or faulty equipment
Cut gun cable, cracked work clamp, gas leak, regulator that will not hold its setting, machine that trips or smells of burning
Stop, isolate, tag it DO NOT USE, and tell your instructor
Injuries and near misses
Arc eye, a burn, a tingle from the gun, the wire striking someone's hand, a small fire
First aid if needed; report it so it is recorded and the cause is fixed
Materials
Rusty wire, an unlabelled cylinder, gas running low, wrong tips in the box
Report it so it is replaced or reordered
Your job
Welds outside the drawing, faults you could not correct, settings that worked
Record them on the job card or inspection sheet and tell your instructor

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain how MIG welding works and what GMAW, MIG and MAG mean.
I can name the hazards of MIG welding, including UV, fume, shielding gas and the moving wire, and say how to control each one.
I can choose and check my PPE, including a suitable filter shade.
I can explain why a MIG machine is constant voltage and why solid wire runs on DCEP.
I can name the parts of the wire feeder and gun and say what each one does.
I can choose the right shielding gas for mild steel and for aluminium, and say what the gas does.
I can secure a cylinder, fit a regulator/flowmeter, leak-test it and set the flow.
I can read the code ER70S-6.
I can choose the right drive rolls and contact tip, load a spool, thread the wire and set the roll pressure and spool brake.
I can explain what wire feed speed and voltage each do, and set them from a chart and a test on scrap.
I can explain short-circuit, globular and spray transfer and say when each is used.
I can hold the right stick-out and travel and work angles, and say when to push or pull.
I can make butt, lap and tee welds in the flat and horizontal positions.
I can name the common MIG faults, their causes and how to prevent them, including cold lap and burnback.
I can inspect a weld by eye and with a fillet gauge, and record and report what I find.
I can clean and check the gun and machine, shut down safely, and report faults.

c1.title: A utility trailer in Old Harbour
c1.text: Rushane is MIG welding a utility trailer frame at a shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine, using 0.9 mm ER70S-6 wire and an argon/CO2 mix. The frame is 50 mm × 50 mm square tube with a 3 mm wall, and the drawbar is joined to 6 mm plate. It is a hot afternoon: the roller door is open to the sea breeze, and a large standing fan blows across the bench. His welds are full of small holes, so he has turned the gas flow up to 30 litres per minute.

c2.title: Changing the wire in Montego Bay
c2.text: Shantel works at a fabrication shop in Montego Bay, St James. She has taken off a spool of 0.8 mm wire and loaded a new spool of 0.9 mm ER70S-6. The drive rolls and the contact tip are the ones that were fitted for the 0.8 mm wire. Between jobs she coils the gun cable in tight loops round the machine's handle. When she releases the trigger, the spool keeps turning and loops of wire spring loose.

c3.title: Hurricane shutter frames at the Centre
c3.text: At a training centre in Kingston, Kemoy is MIG welding frames of 1.6 mm steel sheet for hurricane shutters. He leaves the machine on the settings another trainee used for 6 mm plate, and he burns holes in the sheet. His next job is a base plate of 12 mm steel in the flat position. The shop has only 100% CO2 gas, and he wants to use spray transfer to get the job done quickly.

c4.title: An aluminium rail in Port Antonio
c4.text: Odane is asked to MIG weld a broken aluminium handrail on a fishing boat at a boatyard in Port Antonio, Portland. The shop's MIG machine is set up for steel, with a steel coil liner, V-groove drive rolls and an argon/CO2 mix. The rail is weathered and has a dull grey surface.

c5.title: The gas store in May Pen
c5.text: Garfield's small shop in May Pen, Clarendon, uses CO2 shielding gas. On long welds the regulator frosts over and the welds become porous. The spare cylinders are kept in a small back room with the door shut, and the latest delivery includes a cylinder with no readable label.

questions.q: Which change is most likely to stop the holes in Rushane's welds?
o: Turn the gas up further, to about 40 litres per minute
Turn the fan away from the bench and screen the open door
Change to a larger wire so the arc is too strong for the wind
Weld faster so that the breeze has less time to reach the pool
questions.why: The fan and breeze blow the shielding gas off the pool, so air gets in and causes porosity. Turning fans away and screening the work protects the gas shield; more gas does not.

questions.q: Why can turning the flow up to 30 litres per minute make the porosity worse?
o: The fast, swirling gas can drag air into the shield
The extra gas cools the pool so it sets before the gas escapes
High flow changes the machine from DCEP to DCEN
The argon in the mix turns into an active gas at high flow
questions.why: Too much flow makes the gas stream turbulent, and it sucks air in round the nozzle. Indoor work usually needs about 10–20 L/min; draughts are cured by screening, not more gas.

questions.q: Where should Rushane aim the arc when he welds the 3 mm tube wall to the 6 mm plate?
o: Mostly at the tube wall, because it is the part being joined on
Exactly halfway between, with no bias to either part
Mostly at the plate, so the thin wall is not burned away
Along the top edge of the tube, well above the root of the joint
questions.why: A thin part heats and melts much faster than a thick one. Directing more of the arc onto the 6 mm plate lets both parts fuse without burning through the 3 mm wall.

questions.q: Later, Rushane's fillets come out tall and ropey, and the wire stubs into the plate. What should he change first?
o: Lower the voltage so that the arc is shorter
Lower the gas flow back to 10 litres per minute
Raise the voltage a little to suit the wire speed
Lengthen his stick-out to about 25 mm to calm the arc
questions.why: Stubbing and a tall, ropey bead show the voltage is too low for the wire speed. A little more voltage lengthens the arc and lets the bead wet out into the toes.

questions.q: What must Shantel change now that she has loaded 0.9 mm wire?
o: Only the nozzle, since the wire size makes no other difference
The liner only, because the tip and rolls suit any size
The gas, as 0.9 mm wire needs pure argon to run smoothly
The drive roll groove and the contact tip, to 0.9 mm
questions.why: Rolls and tips are made for one wire size. A 0.8 mm groove squashes 0.9 mm wire, and a 0.8 mm tip will jam it and cause burnback; both must match the new wire.

questions.q: How does coiling the gun cable tightly round the handle affect the welding?
o: The wire drags in the bent liner and feeds poorly
It keeps the liner straight and makes the wire feed faster
It cools the cable so the gun can weld for longer
It has no effect once the cable is uncoiled to weld
questions.why: Tight loops kink and bend the liner, so the wire drags, feeds jerkily and can bird's-nest. Lay the cable out straight while welding and coil it in large, loose loops for storage.

questions.q: What should Shantel adjust so the spool stops cleanly when she releases the trigger?
o: Loosen the drive roll pressure so the wire can slip
Tighten the spool brake a little
Turn the wire feed speed down to its lowest setting
Fit a contact tip one size larger than the wire
questions.why: A spool brake set too light lets the heavy spool run on after the rolls stop, throwing off loose coils. Tighten it just enough to stop the overrun without making the rolls struggle.

questions.q: Shantel's wire keeps melting back and fusing to the tip. She holds the nozzle almost touching the plate. What is the likely cause?
o: Her stick-out is too long, so the wire overheats
The gas flow is too low to cool the tip
Her stick-out is too short for the arc
The work clamp is too close to the joint
questions.why: With the nozzle almost on the plate, the arc burns right up to the tip and the wire fuses to it. About 10 mm of stick-out keeps the tip clear; a jammed or wrong-size tip can also cause burnback.

questions.q: What should Kemoy do to stop burning holes in the 1.6 mm sheet?
o: Raise the voltage so the arc spreads the heat wider
Lower the wire speed and voltage to the chart for 1.6 mm
Change to a 1.2 mm wire so the arc is more stable
Weld more slowly so that each part of the joint fuses fully
questions.why: Settings for 6 mm plate put far too much heat into thin sheet. Start from the chart for the real thickness, test on scrap, and travel steadily; slowing down would add even more heat.

questions.q: Why does the instructor tell Kemoy to use short-circuit transfer on the sheet?
o: It is the only transfer mode that works with an argon/CO2 mix
It needs no shielding gas, so draughts in the shop do not matter
It gives deeper penetration than any other transfer mode
Its low current and small pool put little heat into the sheet
questions.why: Short-circuit transfer runs at low voltage and current, and its small pool freezes quickly. That limits heat, burn-through and distortion on thin sheet, and lets it be used in all positions.

questions.q: Why can Kemoy not get true spray transfer on the 12 mm plate with this gas?
o: Spray transfer needs an argon-rich gas, not pure CO2
Spray transfer only works on plate thinner than 6 mm
CO2 cannot be used for welding steel thicker than 10 mm
Spray needs a constant current machine, not a MIG set
questions.why: Spray transfer needs high current and an argon-rich mix, often about 80% argon or more. With 100% CO2 the metal crosses in large, spattery globules at high current.

questions.q: The long seams on the shutter frames are buckling. Which method will best reduce this?
o: Weld each seam in one long run, as fast as possible
Cool each run with a wet rag as soon as it is made
Tack often and weld in short runs spread along the frame
Turn up the settings so that each seam is finished quicker
questions.why: Short runs spread along the job, with frequent tacks and clamping, stop heat building up in one place. Quenching with water does not prevent shrinkage and can harm the steel.

questions.q: Apart from the gas, what must change on the machine before Odane can feed aluminium wire well?
o: Knurled drive rolls and a shorter gun cable
U-groove drive rolls and a plastic liner
A smaller tip and higher roll pressure
V-groove rolls one size larger than the wire
questions.why: Soft aluminium wire is shaved by V-grooves and drags in a steel liner. U-groove rolls, a plastic (PTFE or nylon) liner and light roll pressure, often with a spool gun, let it feed.

questions.q: How should Odane prepare the weathered rail before welding?
o: Weld through the grey surface, as it melts at a lower heat
Brush it with the steel wire brush used on mild steel
Heat it with a torch until the grey layer burns away
Remove the oxide with a stainless brush kept for aluminium
questions.why: The grey oxide skin melts at a far higher temperature than aluminium and spoils the weld. A stainless brush used only on aluminium removes it without leaving steel particles that cause corrosion.

questions.q: What is the right way to stop Garfield's CO2 regulator freezing?
o: Use a heated CO2 regulator, as the maker supplies
Pour warm water over it whenever frost appears
Lay the cylinder on its side so the gas flows more evenly
Wrap it in rags and tap it with a hammer to free it
questions.why: CO2 cools sharply as it expands, so the regulator can freeze and the flow drops. A heated regulator prevents this; water, hammering or laying the cylinder down are unsafe.

questions.q: What should be done with the cylinder that has no readable label?
o: Use it, since it was delivered with the shop's gas
Do not use it; return it to the supplier
Work out the gas from the colour of the cylinder
Open the valve a little and smell the gas
questions.why: Only the label tells you what is inside, and colours differ between suppliers. An unidentified cylinder is not used; it goes back to the supplier.

questions.q: Where should Garfield keep his spare gas cylinders?
o: In the back room, as long as all the valves are shut tight
Lying on the floor so that they cannot fall over or roll
Upright and chained in a ventilated, shaded place
In the welding bay, next to the machine in use
questions.why: Cylinders are stored upright and secured, where any leak can blow away and heat cannot reach them. A leak in a closed room can push out the oxygen without warning.

questions.q: Which stick-out is about right for short-circuit welding with 0.9 mm wire?
o: About 2 mm
About 10 mm
About 25 mm
About 40 mm
questions.why: Short-circuit work usually uses about 6–12 mm. Much shorter causes spatter on the tip and burnback; much longer lowers the current and weakens the gas cover.

questions.q: Why is ER70S-6 wire often chosen for general shop work on mild steel?
o: Its extra manganese and silicon cope with light rust and scale
It is a flux-cored wire, so it needs no shielding gas at all
It is made to weld stainless steel as well as mild steel plate
It runs on AC, so it suits every kind of welding machine in the shop
questions.why: The -6 wire has more deoxidisers (manganese and silicon) than the -3 wire, so it tolerates light scale and rust better. It is still a solid wire that needs shielding gas, and the joint should still be cleaned.

questions.q: The first 10–15 mm of each of Dwight's MIG fillets sits high and is not fused at the toes; the rest is good. What should he do?
o: Raise the gas flow for the first few seconds of each weld
Start each weld with a much longer stick-out
Grind the plate thinner where each weld begins
Start a little ahead, then come back over the start point
questions.why: The start of a MIG weld is cold because the plate has not yet heated. Striking a little ahead and running back over the start (or pausing briefly) fuses it; a longer stick-out would make it colder still.
